extracted.intended_audience: postsecondary mathematics instructors and mathematics educators (instructors designing & facilitating classroom discussions and assessments)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, enacting, and responding during collaborative problem solving and whole-class discussions in mathematics courses, with emphasis on equity, student status, and assessment practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assigning competence (three components)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigning competence involves: 1) identifying a student perceived as low status, 2) identifying their mathematical contribution, and 3) making that contribution public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying low-status students can be supported by intentional data collection (see Chapter 7). Monitor participation until you identify a mathematical contribution from the target student, then make that contribution public to elevate their status. Be careful not to repeatedly elevate already high-status students (this undermines equity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spotlight
rubrics_metrics.description: Use instructor authority to highlight a particular student's contribution, creating public space for it to be valued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases: “I want to pause for a minute while you think about that idea,” or “I heard something really interesting in the partner share that I want you all to hear.” Avoid spotlighting incorrect ideas unless the classroom has normalized failure and students won't feel shamed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Attach a student's name to a particular idea (e.g., “Katy’s conjecture”) to make it a stable object the class can return to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powerful when you want the class to focus on or revisit an idea across days. Use only to portray the student in a positive light; avoid using this to further boost already high-status students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher press
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask follow-up questions to move student responses along the what–how–why continuum to reveal deeper thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After a surface-level response (e.g., “I got four”), use targeted probing to surface reasoning. Use knowledge from turn-and-talks or small-group work to choose whom and when to press; pressing confused students can feel like negative attention if not timed well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revoice
rubrics_metrics.description: Restate or paraphrase a student's contribution to clarify and publicize their idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May be verbatim repetition (“Jillian said that we need to use Sylow’s theorems”) or paraphrase to make intent clear, then invite class response (“What do you all think of that?”). Revoicing creates space for others to engage and elevates the original contributor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlighting competence (specific praise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly describe the specific mathematical contribution and why it is valuable rather than offering empty praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example scripts: “Devon found two solutions… Having multiple solutions is a great way to deepen understanding,” or “Matias found a clever way to work around the issue….” Be specific about what was contributed (multiple representations, proofs, pushing assumptions) so both idea and student status are elevated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orchestrating discussions (Five Practices overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the five practices—anticipating, monitoring, selecting, sequencing, and connecting—to plan and control whole-class discussions so they appear natural while highlighting target mathematical ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These practices presuppose: introduction of a task, collaborative problem solving, then whole-class discussion. They rely on prior planning and require students to have time to work on the problem before discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipating
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the lesson, anticipate how students will respond to a task, including likely sticking points and productive approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prior teaching notes, samples of student thinking from curricula, or pre-assessments. Anticipation is hard for a task taught for the first time; notes from prior years help. Anticipating enables selection of key mathematical ideas to highlight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring (during group work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe and record student thinking during collaborative problem solving to surface ideas for later discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use questioning strategies to elicit thinking; take notes (e.g., clipboard with group, strategy, sequence columns). Homework can also be used as a monitoring tool. Notes provide the foundation for selecting and sequencing ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose which student ideas to highlight in the whole-class discussion based on your monitoring notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give students advance warning that you may call on them (reduces stress). Offer choices: the student may share, another student from the group can share, you may present the idea for them, or share anonymously. Select ideas that will advance the intended mathematical goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide the order in which student ideas are shared to shape the mathematical narrative and create opportunities for productive struggle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence from less-complete/productive attempts to more-general/correct solutions to foster discussion. Beware of always placing the same group last (this signals status); mix who shares and when to distribute status-raising opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connecting
rubrics_metrics.description: Help students make connections among different groups' ideas to build coherence and link to mathematical practices or learning goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast different approaches (e.g., proof by contradiction vs induction), map one group's representation onto another's, and explicitly relate ideas to larger mathematical practices such as communication or generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-selecting student work before class
rubrics_metrics.description: Select and invite students in advance to share work they prepared outside class (homework/project) to allow more intentional highlighting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: greater intentionality, less on-the-fly cognitive load. If you’ve reviewed homework before class, you can email students asking them to share; options include sharing publicly, having the student present, or sharing anonymously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of notes and artifacts to plan sequencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep structured notes (group, strategy, sequence) while monitoring to support selection and sequencing decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave sequencing column blank while collecting notes, then fill it when you decide the order of strategies to highlight. Notes help ensure you can get ideas out from many groups and plan contrasts that illuminate processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to problematic interactions (venue-matched response)
rubrics_metrics.description: Address negative or identity-based interactions in the same venue they occurred (whole class, small group, or one-on-one) so you do not implicitly condone them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicly address blatant comments in whole-class discussion using community agreements (e.g., “This is an environment for all students to learn, and racist speech is not acceptable here.”). Address small-group slurs within the group; handle after-class disclosures via one-on-one check-ins. Doing nothing implicitly sanctions the behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microintervention strategies (choose response based on strategic goal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select from microintervention techniques (make invisible visible, disarm, educate, or seek external intervention) depending on whether your goal is to surface the issue, disarm the microaggression, educate the offender, or obtain outside help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subtle interventions: rephrase (e.g., use “you all” instead of “you guys”) or offer mild reframing. Stronger interventions: name the behavior (“that’s sexist”) or invoke community standards. Educational approaches: ask inquiry questions to uncover assumptions; consider one-on-one follow-up. For escalation or safety issues, seek external support.

rubrics_metrics.name: RAVEN approach to disrupting microaggressions
rubrics_metrics.description: A five-step, learning-oriented scripted tool: Redirect; Ask probing questions; Values clarification; Emphasize your own thoughts and feelings; Next steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Redirect: interrupt to stop harm (e.g., “let’s pause…”). 2) Ask: clarify intent (e.g., “What do you mean by that?”). 3) Values: link to community agreements (e.g., “this doesn’t sound respectful”). 4) Emphasize: use “I” statements to express impact. 5) Next steps: suggest remediation (apology, commitment, education). RAVEN is practiceable and aims to understand/educate/diffuse rather than escalate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling severe incidents and safety-first responses
rubrics_metrics.description: For incidents beyond in-the-moment handling (e.g., potential physical altercations), prioritize safety, separate students, and seek external institutional support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate goal: keep the classroom safe and maintain focus for others. Example: remove and separate students, suspend their participation for the session, then follow up later with administration and individual conversations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment frames what counts; choose meaningful, accessible problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment communicates “what counts” in a course; choose meaningful tasks and ensure linguistic, cultural, and other elements are accessible to all students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If assessment is narrowly defined (e.g., timed computational exams), students will infer that math is about speed and procedure. Use a wider variety of assessment opportunities that allow students to express understanding in multiple ways; align tasks with intended learning outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disentangle grading and feedback; incorporate feedback throughout
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat assessment as a mechanism to surface thinking and generate feedback; separate grading (sorting) from feedback (learning support) and incorporate feedback continuously within the learning cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feedback should be used during the learning process rather than only after high-stakes grading. Grades often sustain hierarchies (sorting students into tracks); use formative assessment and in-process feedback to promote deeper learning and equity.
